newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges N. Ireland investment despite bomb.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges N. Ireland investment despite bomb.

text.p: U.S. officials at an Irish business conference on Tuesday condemned the bombing of the British army's headquarters in Northern Ireland but said it should not deter U.S. investment.

Stuart Eizenstat, Commerce Department undersecretary, said "we doubled everybody's determination to make sure that we're not going to let a bomb here or there deter what otherwise would be a very wise business decision."
He added, "we condemn in strongest ways this outrage ... We remain hopeful that other groups will not allow themselves to be goaded into a spiraling cycle of retaliation."

A double car bomb attack on Monday at British army headquarters in Lisburn, near Belfast, injured 31 people. Britain said the Irish Republican Army was the prime suspect but an unconfirmed report also said a maverick group, the Irish Continuity Army Council, claimed responsibility.

Eizenstat said despite the shaky peace process between Britain and Ireland, Northern Ireland is a wise place for U.S. firms to invest because of a young and educated work force, competitive wage rates, and access to European markets.

He was speaking at the U.S. Conference on Trade and Investment in Northern Ireland and the Border Counties of Ireland, which was held this week in Pittsburgh. The event brought together some 200 U.S. and Irish companies to discuss investment and trade opportunities.
Eizenstat said conference attendees were undeterred from investing in Northern Ireland despite the bombing and he expected new business ventures to result from the conference.

"I think businesses recognize that there are no totally safe places in the world," he said. "We already have some $850 million of U.S. investment in Northern Ireland ... we're not starting from a completely clean slate."

Baroness Jean Denton of Wakefield, parliamentary undersecretary of state in Britain's Northern Ireland office of Economic Development and Agriculture, said U.S. manufacturing facilities in the region have been profitable, but conceded that a bombing "makes our marketing job harder."

"If we can get companies to visit Northern Ireland, there isn't a (political) issue," she said. "The important thing to remember after a tragedy like yesterday is, 'Does it change the strength of the economic package?"
